w: London's second-largest Royal Park after Richmond, 445 hectares immediately north of Hampton Court Palace, a short walk from Kingston Bridge. Since 2014 it's protected, with Hampton Court Park and Golf Course, as a biological Site of Special Scientific Interest, and Grade I listed as a historic park.
_facts: 445 hectares (1,100 acres); second-largest Royal Park after Richmond Park
Immediately north of Hampton Court Palace
Grade I listed on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens; part of an SSSI since 2014

w: The present crossing here opened in 1903 as King Edward VII Bridge, the king and Queen Alexandra on hand, linking Richmond upon Thames to Hounslow across the tidal Thames. Engineers John Wolfe-Barry and Cuthbert Brereton designed its wide stone spans; Historic England listed it Grade II in 1983.
s: 1903 royal bridge over the tidal Thames
_facts: Opened 1903 as King Edward VII Bridge by the King and Queen Alexandra
Designed by John Wolfe-Barry and Cuthbert Arthur Brereton
Grade II listed in 1983; links the boroughs of Richmond upon Thames and Hounslow

w: George III founded this observatory to track the sky and the Earth's magnetic field from what was then Kew; Sir William Chambers designed the building, and his layout went on to shape two Irish observatories, Armagh and Dunsink near Dublin. Grade I listed, it is now a private house, its instruments long gone.
s: George III's observatory, now a private house
_facts: Founded by King George III as an astronomical and terrestrial magnetic observatory
Chambers's design influenced Armagh Observatory and Dunsink Observatory in Ireland
Grade I listed; now a private dwelling, formerly known as Kew Observatory

w: The only Thames lock owned by the Port of London Authority, opened 1894 to hold the lowest head of water of the forty-five navigable Thames reaches. At high tide its sluice gates rise, hidden behind twin metal arches that double as footbridges linking Richmond to St Margarets -- shut to walkers after 7:30pm.
s: Thames lock whose sluices double as footbridges
_facts: Opened 1894; the only Thames lock owned and operated by the Port of London Authority
Sluice gates rise at high tide, forming twin footbridges between Richmond and St Margarets
Closed to pedestrians after 19:30 GMT (21:30 BST)
